records.our_prose: For a tree, companions really means root-zone management, not vegetable pairing. Keep lawn grass and weeds cleared out to the drip line: turf competes hard for water and nitrogen and slows a young lime, and string trimmers used to fight grass at the trunk nick the tender bark. Keep organic mulch pulled back at least a foot from the trunk to reduce Phytophthora foot-rot risk. Limes are self-fruitful, so no second tree is needed for pollination. UF/IFAS also cautions against heavy lawn fertilization and herbicide drift near citrus. Low, shallow-rooted plantings well outside the drip line are harmless; anything crowding the trunk or holding moisture against it is not. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, Texas A&M AgriLife.)

records.our_prose: Limes prefer a slightly acidic soil around pH 6.0 to 6.5 but tolerate a broad range (roughly 5.5 to 8.0), including the alkaline calcareous soils of the Florida Keys and rockland. records.our_prose: Limes need little pruning. Do any shaping or thinning in late winter to early spring before the new flush, never in fall (which pushes tender growth into cold that a tender lime cannot afford) and never a hard dormant-season cut (the tree is never dormant). Remove dead, crossing, or frost-damaged wood, and always strip shoots arising below the graft union, which come from the rootstock. Wait for spring regrowth before cutting freeze-damaged wood, so you can see what survived.

records.our_prose: Limes need well-drained soil above all else: they do not tolerate flooded conditions, and poor drainage invites Phytophthora foot rot. They grow well in sand and in the shallow calcareous rocklands of south Florida, but sharp drainage is the constant. Plant on a raised mound or bed on heavy clay, set the tree so the graft union sits well above grade, and never dig a watering basin that holds water against the trunk. Keep organic mulch at least a foot from the trunk. On alkaline or calcareous soils, plan on nutritional micronutrient sprays and chelated iron. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
